paper.title: Mitigating Bias in Locally Constrained Decoding via Tractable Proposals

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1-7 and Appendices A (LCD bias example), B (HMMs)

claims.claim: Constrained decoding for language models can guarantee that every output satisfies a constraint given as a finite automaton within a fixed token budget, which today's standard practice of masking only tokens that immediately break the constraint does not, at almost no extra decoding cost, by running the automaton as tensor operations on the GPU and masking any token after which no valid completion fits in the remaining budget. Supported only if, on function-calling outputs required to match a JSON schema or a Python-like call syntax with a 128-token budget, this masking yields 100% valid outputs at every particle budget tested while immediate-violation masking leaves some outputs invalid; if its per-token latency is within 1.2 times that of unconstrained generation; and if it works directly with nondeterministic automata, which for realistic schemas and SQL grammar are far smaller than the equivalent deterministic ones.
claims.decision_rule: GCD 100% constraint satisfaction on xLAM JSON and Python-like vs LCD < 100%; latency <= 1.2x unconstrained; NFA support where DFA blows up.

claims.claim: When sampling from a language model conditioned on a hard constraint with sequential Monte Carlo, proposals that mask by reachability of a valid completion within the budget, and especially ones that also weight tokens by a hidden Markov model's estimate of how likely a valid completion is, approach the true conditional distribution with far fewer particles than proposals built from immediate-violation masking. Supported only if, at the same number of particles (from 4 up), both proposals give higher task accuracy than the immediate-masking proposal on JSON and Python-like function calling and on text-to-SQL, and the probabilistic proposal converges faster than the purely logical one; if using the probabilistic estimate also as the SMC potential improves keyword-constrained generation further; and if even a small hidden Markov model already helps.
claims.decision_rule: Higher accuracy than LCD+SMC at equal k>=4 on xLAM (JSON, Python) and Spider; P-GCD converges faster than GCD; phi-PGCD improves CommonGen BLEU; small HMM (H=1024) beats LCD at k>=2.

experiments.text: Turn constraints into tensors and define the samplers. Setup: compile each constraint into a finite automaton (deterministic or not), group transitions into edges labelled by token sets, and encode it as binary source, destination and edge-label matrices. A forward pass over these matrices gives, for every vocabulary token at once, the states reached; a backward pass precomputed from the accepting states gives which states can still accept in exactly the remaining steps; their product is the token mask. For the probabilistic version, distil a hidden Markov model from samples of the language model (2M samples, about 2 H100 hours, plus 0.2-3 hours of training for 1,024-16,384 hidden states) and multiply it with the automaton viewed as a hidden Markov model over edges, so that the product gives the HMM's probability of the next token given that the constraint will be met. Compare as sequential Monte Carlo proposals: immediate-violation masking (as in Outlines and XGrammar), budget-aware masking, and the probabilistic proposal (mixing language-model and HMM next-token probabilities), with rejection sampling from the unconstrained model as ground truth.

Measure how often outputs satisfy the constraint. Setup: 1,000 test examples sampled from the xLAM function-calling dataset after removing examples whose reference answer violates its own function specification; JSON-schema and Python-like call formats; token budget 128; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Result: immediate-violation masking gives 95.26% and 95.40% valid outputs at 4 and 16 particles in JSON and 98.12% and 99.20% in Python-like syntax (for example by opening braces it never closes before the budget runs out), while budget-aware and probabilistic masking give 100.0% in every setting.

Measure decoding cost. Setup: wall-clock milliseconds per token on one H100 over 100 xLAM examples, batch 16, mean over 3 seeds. Result: unconstrained 1.69 ms, immediate-violation masking 1.83 ms (1.08x), budget-aware masking 1.86 ms (1.10x); the probabilistic version costs 5.26-17.30 ms (3.11-10.2x) for hidden sizes 1,024-16,384.

Show why nondeterministic automata matter. Setup: a function whose schema requires at least one of n pairs of arguments, and the SQL grammar used for Spider; count states of the nondeterministic automaton and of the minimal deterministic one. Result: for the function schema the nondeterministic automaton grows linearly in n while the deterministic one grows exponentially; for SQL, 7,999 versus 57,263 states at character level and 31,858 versus out-of-memory at token level.

Compare proposals at equal particle counts on function calling. Setup: xLAM JSON and Python-like formats, accuracy meaning the call parses and has the correct function and arguments, as a function of the number of SMC particles, with rejection sampling as the target. Result: both new proposals reach higher accuracy than immediate-violation masking at the same particle count and approach the rejection-sampling accuracy much faster, the probabilistic proposal fastest; immediate masking with SMC plateaus at 69.7% (JSON) at 8-16 particles.

Check how good the hidden Markov model must be. Setup: xLAM JSON accuracy for immediate masking and for the probabilistic proposal with hidden sizes 1,024 and 16,384 at 1-16 particles. Result: immediate masking 66.4 / 68.2 / 69.3 / 69.7 / 69.7% at 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 particles; small HMM 65.4 / 68.6 / 70.2 / 71.1 / 71.5%; large HMM 66.5 / 69.2 / 70.5 / 71.5 / 71.6%. The small HMM is slightly worse with one particle but better from two, and the gap between HMM sizes shrinks as particles increase.

Test on SQL generation with a nondeterministic grammar. Setup: 500 Spider examples, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, HMM with 1,024 states distilled on the remaining data, token budget 128, execution accuracy (same result as the reference query on the database). Result: at 1 / 4 / 8 particles, 59.8 / 65.4 / 67.2% for immediate masking, 59.0 / 66.8 / 69.0% for budget-aware masking and 56.2 / 67.9 / 69.1% for the probabilistic proposal, so both are better from 4 particles but slightly worse with a single particle, which gets no resampling correction.

Test the probabilistic estimate as an SMC potential on keyword-constrained generation. Setup: CommonGen (sentences that must contain 3-5 given concepts, any inflection), GPT2-Large with a released HMM, token budget 32, expected BLEU-4 weighted over particles, comparing language-model likelihood as potential with immediate and budget-aware proposals against the probabilistic proposal plus the probabilistic potential. Result: adding the probabilistic potential converges faster and gives a substantial BLEU advantage over the immediate-masking proposal across particle counts.

notes: Several results are reported only as figures (xLAM accuracy curves, CommonGen BLEU); experiment texts state the qualitative result without inventing numbers.
